TAIEX swings from record weekly loss to record gain
sum: TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The benchmark stock index on Friday posted its largest weekly gain on record, after suffering its heaviest weekly loss last week.

The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, climbed as much as 1,397.61 points intraday to 44,489.48. It closed up 583.25 points, or 1.35%, at 43,675.12, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.

Turnover totaled NT$916.3 billion (US$27.9 billion), down from NT$1.01 trillion in the previous session. The market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$143.07 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

The index ended a four-week losing streak, adding a record 3,973.48 points, or 10.01%, over the week. The recovery followed a 5,510-point decline the previous week, reflecting unusually wide price swings and intense competition between buyers and sellers, according to CTEE.
Most of the market's largest weighted stocks finished higher. TSMC rose 0.43% to NT$2,350.
MediaTek gained 7.01% to NT$4,120, while Foxconn edged up 0.42% to NT$241. Delta Electronics was unchanged at NT$1,240, and ASE added 2.05% to NT$598, according to Yahoo Stocks.

Global Unichip overtook server rail maker King Slide Works to become the TAIEX's second-highest-priced stock. The chip designer touched its daily limit-up of NT$8,645 during the session before ending 9.54% higher at NT$8,610. King Slide lost 3.49% to NT$7,880.

sum: The Taiwan stock market's weighted index (TAIEX) surged to an intraday high of 44,525.24 points on Wednesday (Nov. 12), extending a rebound of more than 6,600 points over four trading sessions from the Nov. 6 intraday low of 37,837.05. But sentiment reversed in the afternoon as selling pressure swept across the board, and the index closed down 1,165.28 points, or 2.63%, at 43,091.87. Turnover reached NT$1.0133 trillion (approximately $30.7 billion). Market heavyweight Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) weakened in tandem, closing at NT$2,340, down NT$55 or 2.3%, and was the main drag on the broader market.

The sharp swing has prompted the market to reassess the actual effectiveness of the National Stabilization Fund's support. Chen Jia-wei, vice president of Chengtong Investment Consulting, said on his personal YouTube channel that in the past the fund has mostly entered when the index was near relatively low levels such as the five-year moving average or even the ten-year line, but this time it acted early near the annual line, breaking with precedent. Based on Taiwan Stock Exchange closing data, the 240-day annual line stood at about 38,835 points on Nov. 6, and that day's close of 39,701.64 was only 2.2% above it; the intraday low of 37,837.05 was about 1,000 points below the annual line—consistent with his description of "near the annual line." He argued that if the market trend continues downward, even capital deployed for support may not reverse the bearish course, and the effect could fall short of market expectations.

sum: U.S. stocks closed broadly higher on Wednesday (the 11th), driven by strong earnings from cloud-computing startup CoreWeave and Nvidia's share price stabilizing, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index surging 5.66%. But Taiwan stocks did not follow through on Thursday (the 12th). The TAIEX opened down 76.69 points at 44,180.46 and repeatedly swung between gains and losses, hitting an intraday high of 44,427.51 and a low of 43,878.52 — a drop of more than 300 points and a swing of over 500 points. Bellwether Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) opened at NT$2,385, down NT$10, and touched an intraday low of NT$2,355, a decline of more than 1%, falling back below its monthly and half-year moving averages.

CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue rose 168% year over year to $3.66 billion, and the company raised its full-year guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion (about NT$440 billion), while also lifting its adjusted operating income target to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion. Both revenue and profit forecasts beat market expectations, and the company expects to turn adjusted-profit positive in the first half of 2028. The results eased investor concerns about whether the artificial intelligence (AI) boom can be sustained and finally lifted Nvidia's shares after several days of declines.

All four major U.S. indexes closed higher Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49; the S&P 500 gained 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38, still 2.55% below its record close of 7,818.93 on Oct. 6; the Nasdaq climbed 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19; and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped 565.78 points, or 5.66%, to 10,564.11.

TSMC's ADR surged $16.87 (about NT$550) Wednesday to close at $413.35, a gain of 4.25%, but the local shares failed to carry that momentum on Thursday. TSMC announced Tuesday evening that it would subscribe to $500 million (about NT$16 billion) each of Anthropic common stock and OpenAI preferred stock, and raised its quarterly dividend from NT$7 to NT$9. October consolidated revenue came in at NT$586.89 billion (approximately $17.8 billion), up 14.7% month over month and 59.7% year over year, a record for a single month.

Taiwan stocks jump as regulators curb short selling and deploy a stabilization fund
sum: When a market's regulators cap short selling and send in state money in the same week, the selloff has stopped being a normal correction. If you hold anything in the AI chip chain, Taiwan's rescue is the clearest stress reading you'll get.

Taiwan's Taiex rose as much as 5% on Monday, November 9, its biggest jump since July 31, after authorities moved to stop a rout that had pushed the index into a bear market, Bloomberg reported. The rally ended a seven-session losing run, the longest since 2022. TSMC and MediaTek, the two heaviest AI-linked names on the island, each rose at least 5% in early trading.

Two measures did the work. The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the cap on intraday short-sale orders for borrowed shares to 3% of a stock's 30-day average daily volume, down from 30%, and raised the minimum margin for short sales to 130% from 90%, according to Bloomberg. Alongside that, the government activated the National Financial Stabilization Fund, which Taiwan's government authorised on Friday, November 6, with NT$500 billion available to buy stocks, as reported by The Online Citizen and MLQ. BigGo Finance counted it as the fund's tenth market-support operation.

The Taiex closed on November 6 at 39,701.64, down 1,873 points or 4.51%, according to the Taipei Times. That was the fourth-largest single-day point loss on record, and it was a good day compared with where the session had been. At the low the index was down more than 3,700 points, the largest intraday point drop in its history, before bargain hunters stepped in around noon. Moore Securities analyst Adam Lin told the paper that the buying eased the selling pressure.

TSMC tells the same story in miniature. It fell about 10% at one point on Friday and closed down 4.69% at NT$2,135. The company makes up more than 40% of the market's total value, so when it wobbles the whole index goes with it. BigGo Finance put the week's damage at 5,510 points, a drop of more than 12%, and roughly NT$18 trillion of market value wiped out.
South Korea's Kospi is up 90% this year and Taiwan's TAIEX has hit record highs, both driven almost entirely by Samsung, SK Hynix, and TSMC.

sum: Taiwan has authorised its NT$500 billion National Stabilization Fund and curbed short selling after the TAIEX suffered its largest intraday points drop on record, closing 4.51 per cent lower and entering bear market territory.
- Taiwan authorised its NT$500 billion National Stabilization Fund after the TAIEX’s largest-ever intraday points drop.
- The FSC will curb short selling from 9 November and urged listed companies to buy back shares.
- The TAIEX has fallen 20.55 per cent from its October high, entering bear market territory.

Taiwan’s government on Friday, 6 November 2026, authorised the activation of its NT$500 billion (US$15.26 billion) National Stabilization Fund (NSF) to support local shares, after the TAIEX suffered the largest intraday points drop in its history.

The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) separately announced temporary curbs on short selling, taking effect on Monday, 9 November 2026. It also urged listed companies to buy back their own shares to help restore investor confidence.
The TAIEX plunged 3,737.67 points, or about 9 per cent, in early trading before paring losses to close down 1,873.08 points, or 4.51 per cent, at 39,701.64.

Taiwan Stocks Plunge 9% in a Single Day, Yet Leveraged ETFs Command a Surprising 5% Premium; Margin Positions Swell by 158,000 Lots in Five Days
sum: Taiwan stocks met devastating selling pressure at the open on the 6th, with the Taiwan Weighted Index plunging as much as 3,737 points, or 9%, to 37,837.05 — a rare intraday rout for a single session. Yet amid the panic selling, Taiwan-tracking 2X leveraged ETFs bucked the trend with unusually large premiums: Yuanta Taiwan 50 2X (00631L) saw its intraday premium reach 5.04%, while Capital TAIEX 2X (00685L) and Fubon TAIEX 2X (00675L) reached 4.59% and 3.09%, respectively, showing that a flood of money was buying at prices above net asset value to bet on a short-term rebound.

As of 10:50 a.m., 00631L was down 5.41%, or NT$1.58, at NT$27.63; 00685L was down 5.58%, or NT$0.53, at NT$8.97; and 00675L was down NT$13.50, or 5.39%, at NT$236.80. Against the benchmark's roughly 9% decline, the 2X ETFs' paper losses were comparatively milder. Market commentary indicated this was one of the main reasons the premiums widened, as buying poured in far faster than the funds' net asset values fell.

The premium phenomenon set off a fierce two-sided debate on online investment forums. One investor said bluntly, "Too many gamblers — the 2X funds are being bought straight into premium; this time they're doomed," arguing that buying at a premium amounts to taking a loss up front. Others mocked, "The gamblers aren't panicked enough yet" and "Missing out on gains hurts more than losing money — not catching the big rebound is a loss." Another camp worried that international market variables over the weekend were unpredictable: "With a premium that big, I don't even want to buy — Monday could see another selloff," and "Don't rush in yet, there's still a wave of forced liquidations coming," believing Taiwan stocks still have room to fall in the near term.

Notably, the frenzy of buying in leveraged ETFs did not begin on the 6th. According to statistics, margin balances for 00631L and 00685L combined surged by 158,000 lots over the past five trading sessions, with 00631L adding 37,790 lots in a single day — the highest among all listed stocks and ETFs — and 00685L adding 32,213 lots the same day. In other words, well before the index's string of steep declines, retail investors had already made large margin bets on a rebound.

sum: Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index plunged 4.39% on Wednesday, closing at 42,946.35 in a bruising session that saw substantial losses across the board. The steep decline erased significant recent gains and rattled investors on the island.

The index swung across a wide range during the day, touching a session high of 43,741.54 before selling pressure intensified and dragged it to a low of 41,855.82 — a intraday swing of nearly 1,886 points that underscored the volatility gripping the market. The closing level represented a recovery from the day's trough but remained deeply in negative territory.

None of the domestic headlines circulating during Wednesday's session clearly accounted for a move of this magnitude. The sell-off appeared broad-based, with the market absorbing significant downward pressure throughout the trading day.

The scale of the decline — approaching 4.4% in a single session — marks one of the more severe single-day drops for the TAIEX in recent memory, and analysts will be watching closely to see whether support can be established at current levels or whether further weakness lies ahead.

sum: Taiwan stocks opened lower and fell further on Thursday (the 30th), plunging more than 1,000 points intraday, with the currency market coming under simultaneous pressure. The Taiwan dollar opened at NT$32.52 against the US dollar, down 2.8 cents, before its decline rapidly widened, successively breaking through the NT$32.5 and NT$32.6 barriers and touching a low of NT$32.666 — a sharp drop of 1.74 cents — before consolidating in the NT$32.66 to NT$32.666 range, a textbook case of stocks and the currency falling in tandem.

In international currency markets, the US Dollar Index weakened today, falling below the 102 mark and sliding further from 101.91 to 101.6, while most major Asian currencies strengthened. The Japanese yen rose against the US dollar from 157.892 in early trading to 157.189, the South Korean won also climbed from 1,340.55 to 1,336.78, and the offshore Chinese yuan traded in a range between 6.6573 and 6.6536. Against a backdrop of a softer dollar and a broad rebound in Asian currencies, the Taiwan dollar weakened on its own, highlighting that domestic funding pressure is the main driver of this depreciation wave.

The sharp currency slide has clear roots. The previous day, the Taiwan dollar had just ended a two-session winning streak, closing Thursday at NT$32.492, down 7.4 cents from the prior session, with an interbank high of NT$32.390 and a low of NT$32.597, on turnover of $2.824 billion (approximately NT$92 billion). That day, Taiwanese stocks turned lower after two days of gains, with the TAIEX falling 1.42%, and Foreign Investors sold a net NT$68.81 billion (approximately $2.1 billion) of listed shares, already planting depreciation pressure on the currency.

The scale of capital outflows is a key focus. Taiwan's central bank previously reported that Foreign Investors sold a net $19.402 billion (approximately NT$630 billion) of Taiwanese stocks and recorded net outflows of $17.961 billion (approximately NT$590 billion) between October 12 and 16, driving a 1.37% depreciation of the Taiwan dollar over the same period — showing that Foreign Investor flows continue to sway Taiwanese stocks and the currency.

sum: NEW YORK — Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry bounced back on Wall Street Monday and recovered some of their steep losses from last week, but the rest of the market and stocks worldwide were shaky.

The S&P 500 rose 0.4%, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1% because it's full of technology stocks. The majority of U.S. stocks outside of AI and tech fell, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average swung between losses and gains before finishing with a drop of 36 points, or 0.1%.

In Europe, the losses were sharper, and indexes slid more than 1% following violent protests that could ultimately force the French government to increase its spending to ease voters' anger. That in turn could put even more pressure on bond markets, and yields cranked higher worldwide.

Even with all the cross currents flowing through financial markets, AI stocks stood out, as they have for most of the past few years. A frenzy in spending for AI technology has forced them to the forefront of the market, sending them to record prices and driving indexes higher. Last week, AI stocks grabbed the spotlight after tumbling on worries about how expensive it has become to borrow money, which could threaten the boom.

Much of the spending on AI chips and data centers has come from borrowed money, and Treasury yields in the bond market have recently hit their highest levels in years or even decades. That has raised the cost of borrowing money for everyone.

Nvidia added 1.4% Monday and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total market value, a 1% move for its stock has more effect on the index than any other’s.

sum: South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months.

The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year.
The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom.

In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added.
Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain.

South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry.

Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions.

items.t: Taiwan dethrones South Korea as world market leader amid widening AI trade
sum: As equity investors enter the final stretch of a pivotal year that has propelled South Korea and Taiwan to the forefront of the global artificial intelligence (AI) trade, the latter is emerging as the stronger bet.

The TAIEX beat the KOSPI by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Earnings upgrades also outpaced those for its South Korean peer for the first time since March last year. About 40 percent of the fund managers surveyed by Bank of America Corp last month said they were overweight Taiwan, versus 25 percent for South Korea.
Driving the optimism are Taiwan’s deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.

“The distinction for us is not simply the amount of AI exposure, but the nature of the earnings supporting it,” M&G Investments (Singapore) Pte Ltd portfolio manager Vikas Pershad said. “Taiwan offers a broader and deeper opportunity set. Its earnings come from volume and that makes its earnings upgrades broader and stickier. [South] Korea’s earnings, in the near-term, are coming from price.”

Taiwan offers investors exposure across chip design and manufacturing, packaging, networking and servers, meaning it has more ways to benefit as AI spending broadens. Meanwhile, South Korea’s market leadership remains heavily concentrated in chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, leaving it more vulnerable as doubts emerge over how much longer the current memory upcycle can run.

Up 72 percent this year, the TAIEX is the top performer among more than 90 equity indexes tracked by Bloomberg. The KOSPI is ranked second, with gains of about 63 percent. Taiwan’s lead comes as shares of KOSPI heavyweights Samsung and SK Hynix plunged between 19 percent and 33 percent last quarter.
Earnings estimates for the TAIEX rose about 19 percent in the last quarter, compared with an increase of about 15 percent for the KOSPI, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.

Rules on cooling period for disposition stocks eased
sum: Taipei, Aug. 4 (CNA) The Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) has eased the rules governing the cooling period for "disposition stocks," effective from Aug. 10.
According to the TWSE, the cooling period for a stock placed in disposition will be shortened to five trading sessions from the current 10 trading sessions.
The matching interval will be cut to two minutes from five minutes for a stock which is designated as a disposition stock for the first time.
For stocks designated as disposition stocks for the second time, the matching interval will also be shortened to two minutes from 20 minutes, the TWSE said.

Disposition stocks are those that have shown extreme volatility and are subject to trading restrictions to cool them down. Those restrictions can include using manual rather than automatic matching of buy and sell offers and increasing the matching interval.

In Taiwan, for example, a stock that rises or falls more than 25 percent in six trading sessions, whose accumulated turnaround rate tops 50 percent in six trading sessions, whose single session turnaround rate tops 5 percent, or whose single session turnover stands at over 5-fold the average in the previous 60 sessions is placed on a watch list.

A stock is designated as a disposition stock if those conditions persist for three consecutive trading sessions, for six trading sessions within the last 10 trading days, or for 12 trading days within the last 30 trading days.

sum: On July 16, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) reported second-quarter revenue of US$40.2 billion and a gross margin of 67.7 percent, supported by global demand for AI chips. The following day, the TAIEX (台股加權指數) recorded its largest-ever single-day point decline.

The Index fell 2,953.71 points, or 6.47 percent, as foreign institutional investors sold a net NT$189.04 billion in shares. TSMC fell NT$180. Meanwhile, local individuals set a record for odd-lot trading, buying quantities smaller than the standard 1,000-share lot.
So, why were strong AI earnings followed by a market seizure?

The answer lies in how artificial intelligence has rewired Taiwan’s financial system. The AI boom has increased the exchange’s value, but also concentrated market weight in a few firms, strengthened the link to Wall Street and made local retail investors more important during sudden sell-offs.

The AI rally has also transformed Taiwan into a global stock-market heavyweight. In late June, its listed companies reached a combined value of US$5.22 trillion, briefly placing Taiwan fourth worldwide in a MarketCapWatch ranking cited by the Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE 臺灣證券交易所).
That rise was extraordinary for an economy of Taiwan’s size, but it also reflected the concentration that makes the market vulnerable.

By May, TSMC accounted for 43.8 percent of the market capitalization of companies listed on the stock market. Together with Delta Electronics (台達電) and MediaTek (聯發科), the three represented 52 percent.

The decline dragged Taiwan's Taiex down 6.5%, taking its decline from a June high to nearly 11%. Foreign funds sold US$5.8 billion ($7.5 billion) worth of shares on a net basis on Friday, the most on record, Bloomberg compiled data showed.
A Bloomberg index of Asian chip stocks tumbled more than 6%, led by losses in Kioxia Holdings Corp, a Japanese flash memory maker whose shares have lost half of their value in recent weeks.

The market was also caught off guard by Chinese AI pioneer Moonshot's new model, which it says performs on a par with leading offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC, fuelling concerns that training advanced AI models may require fewer chips.

Stocks falling in the wake of good results "means the market is looking to rotate out of chips and into other things, at least for now", said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital Ltd. "Also the multiples have gotten stretched, so Kioxia going down 50% doesn't even make it cheap yet," he added.

items.t: Taiex ends little changed as TSMC's rebound erases earlier losses
Taiwan shares end up after U.S. rally on eased inflation
sum: Taipei, July 15 (CNA) Shares in Taiwan bounced back Wednesday from a slump a session earlier, with buying sparked by a rally in the United States overnight after slower-than-expected June inflation, dealers said.

The Taiex, the Taiwan Stock Exchange's benchmark index, ended up 893.64 points, or 2.00 percent, at 45,631.59 after moving between 44,850.69 and 45,881.91. Turnover totaled NT$984.08 billion (US$30.61 billion), down from an average of NT$1.06 trillion in the previous five sessions.

items.t: TAIEX drops 1.42% as investors assess geopolitical risks and upcoming TSMC outlook
sum: TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index fell on Tuesday as concerns over Middle East tensions weighed on global markets.

Several stocks that remained above the NT$1,000 threshold, including Mpi, Global Unichip, Alchip Technologies, Landmark Optoelectronics, and Keystone Microtech, hit their daily limit-downs during trading, according to CTEE.

Drone-related stocks moved against the broader market trend, supported by expectations for continued demand from defense and industrial applications. Hocheng, Chenfull International, and Asia Air reached daily limit-ups, while Aerospace Industrial Development and Thunder Tiger also posted notable gains.

items.t: Taiex under heavy pressure but late rebound caps fall

items.t: Taiex ends down as earlier gains eroded amid Middle East concerns

items.t: Taiwan Stocks See Glimmer of Hope After 1,000-Point Plunge? TAIEX Futures Rebound Past 46,000 in Night Session
sum: After a dramatic session on July 7 that saw intraday swings exceeding 1,500 points, Taiwan's night session futures were the first to flash signs of stabilization. TAIEX futures opened the night session on the evening of July 7 at 45,965 points, up 270 points, and briefly surged past the 46,000-point threshold, reaching an intraday high of 46,003 points — a gain of 308 points. Although short-term selling pressure subsequently pushed the index back toward the 45,500-point area, it remained at 45,722 points, up 27 points, as of 9:22 p.m., demonstrating a resilient bid from the bulls.

TSMC had rallied strongly by NT$40 to NT$2,500 in early trading, but as the broader market turned negative around 11 a.m., even the heavyweight leader could not withstand the selling pressure. A final block trade of 3,721 shares at the close pushed the stock to end at NT$2,440, down NT$20 or 0.81%. TSMC alone accounted for roughly 155 points of the TAIEX's decline. Delta Electronics (2308) similarly opened higher before reversing course, ultimately plunging NT$105, or 5.26%, to close at NT$1,890, dragging the index down by approximately 85 points.

The TAIEX ultimately closed at 45,479.11, down 1,077.28 points or 2.31%, on massive turnover of NT$1.17 trillion (approximately $36.4 billion).

Taiwan Stocks Surge While Foreign Investors Dump Over NT$800 Billion in Shares; First-Half Net Inward Remittance Hits Record NT$2.44 Trillion
sum: Taiwan's stock market staged a liquidity-driven rally in the first half of 2026, with the TAIEX surging more than 60%. However, foreign investors were net sellers during the same period, offloading more than NT$835.6 billion (approximately $26.1 billion) in shares, the second-largest cumulative net sell-off for the period since 2022. Yet this selling pressure did not stem the tide of capital inflows. The latest statistics from Taiwan's FSC show that cumulative net inward remittances by foreign investors reached $76.78 billion in the first half, equivalent to approximately NT$2.44 trillion, rewriting the historical record for the same period and creating a peculiar dynamic of "selling stocks with one hand while wiring in money with the other."

According to data released by the FSC's Securities and Futures Bureau, foreign investors (including mainland Chinese capital) sold a net NT$570.68 billion (approximately $17.8 billion) in listed and over-the-counter stocks in June alone. This was not only the largest net sell-off for the month of June on record but also the second-largest single-month net sell-off since 2022. Cumulatively, in the first six months of 2026, foreign investors withdrew NT$835.64 billion (approximately $26.1 billion) from Taiwan's stock market, indicating that even as the TAIEX hit an all-time high of 48,218 points, foreign investors opted to lock in profits at elevated levels.

In the foreign exchange market, however, the momentum of foreign capital inflows showed no signs of abating. FSC statistics indicate that foreign investors recorded a net inward remittance of $11.63 billion in June, equivalent to approximately NT$370.39 billion (approximately $11.6 billion) based on the month-end exchange rate of NT$31.837 per U.S. dollar, setting a new record for the month. For the first half of the year, cumulative net inward remittances reached $76.78 billion, also a record high for the period. As of the end of June, the cumulative balance of foreign capital parked in Taiwan approached $396.94 billion, equivalent to over NT$12 trillion (approximately $375.1 billion).
Market analysts suggest that this contradictory behavior of "selling stocks but not repatriating funds" reflects a broader shift in global capital allocation.

items.t: TSMC Surges NT$85, Igniting Taiwan Stocks to Rocket Over 1,000 Points Past 47,278

Investment firms remain optimistic, with consensus targets near 50,000 points, driven by AI-led earnings expansion. Hong Kong market faces pressure as HK$255 billion in locked shares expire in July
sum: The potential wave of selling poses an additional headwind for the city’s struggling equity market
[HONG KONG] Hong Kong’s underperforming stock market may come under renewed pressure as a large amount of shares frozen under restrictions tied to equities offerings become tradable next month.

At least HK$255 billion (S$41.8 billion) worth of stocks, either from initial public offerings or secondary share sales, will see their temporary lockups expire in July, the most for any month through the rest of this year, according to exchange data calculated by Bloomberg.

Separately, Goldman Sachs Group estimates that IPO-induced lockup expiries in the city will total US$274 billion in the coming year, marking a record for any 12-month period. Shares held by cornerstone investors of a Hong Kong IPO and existing shareholders won’t be available for public trading for a period of time, typically for six months or a year after the stock’s listing.

The looming expiries result from an IPO boom in the financial hub late last year and early this year, when technology firms rushed to capture the artificial intelligence investment frenzy. The potential selling pressure would be an extra headwind for Hong Kong stocks, which have lagged Asian peers such as South Korea and Taiwan that have led the global AI trade.

Pressured by China’s struggling economy and doubts on Chinese firms’ heavy AI spending, the city’s Hang Seng Index has fallen 3 per cent this year, versus an over 100 per cent surge for Korea’s Kospi gauge and the 57 per cent gain for Taiwan’s Taiex benchmark.

“Historical precedents suggest that equities typically experience moderate downward price pressure following lock-up expiration,” Goldman analysts including Si Fu wrote in a note dated on Jun 14. However, both indices do not tell the whole story. Unlike in the past, the rally in these two countries' frontline indices is not broad-based, with only a handful of heavyweights currently driving the market.

For instance, Taiwan's overall market cap has increased by $2.05 trillion to $4.31 trillion from $2.26 trillion since the start of 2025 across its 1,056-stock index. During the same period, the mcap of Taiwan's biggest stock — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — alone rose by $1.04 trillion, making it responsible for more than 50 percent of the total rise in Taiwan's market cap.

The next five stocks — Delta Electronics, MediaTek, ASE Technology Holding, Elite Material, and Unimicron Technology Corp — together contributed around 20 percent to the upward move. On the other hand, the mcap of 549 stocks within the index declined during this period, while another 495 stocks added less than 1 percent to the total.

Similarly, Korea's Kospi mcap has increased by nearly $2.82 trillion to $4.11 trillion from $1.28 trillion across its 835-stock index since the start of 2025. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix saw their market caps rise by $892 billion and $734 billion respectively, making the two stocks together responsible for more than 57 percent of the rise in Kospi's mcap.

The next five stocks — SK Square, Hyundai Motor, Doosan Enerbility, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Hanwha Aerospace — collectively contributed just 10 percent to the move. The mcap of 207 Kospi stocks declined during this period, while nearly 600 stocks contributed less than 1 percent to the total.

Both countries' stock exchanges are the world's biggest outperformers so far in 2026, even as war has broken out between the US, Iran, and Israel with no solution in sight, pushing crude oil prices above $100 per barrel and stoking inflation fears and fiscal pressures for many countries.

sum: Taiwan's stock market is now worth more than the United Kingdom's, according to recent Bloomberg data, in a shift driven almost entirely by the insatiable global appetite for AI chips. The island's listed companies carry a combined valuation of roughly $4.3 trillion, edging past Europe's largest equity market, despite Taiwan's economy being less than a quarter the size of the UK's. South Korea, powered by Samsung and SK hynix, is roughly $140 billion behind and closing fast.

As for Taiwan’s stock market constituents, TSMC makes up the bulk, with a market cap of approximately US$1.98 trillion, or 40% of Taiwan’s entire stock market value. No other major economy has this degree of single-company dependence. By comparison, Apple represents roughly 7% of the S&P 500.

On Thursday, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission raised the single-stock investment cap for local equity funds from 10% to 25% of a fund's net asset value. The change applies only to companies whose market weighting exceeds 10%, a threshold TSMC alone meets. That adjustment triggered a 4.3% jump in TSMC shares on Friday and pushed the benchmark TAIEX up 2.7%, according to Taiwanese media.

TSMC reported record first-quarter earnings last week, with net income up 40.6% year-over-year to roughly $18 billion. The company raised its full-year revenue guidance to more than 30% growth and confirmed plans to add another 3nm fab to meet AI demand, which it expects to outstrip supply through 2027.

South Korea's market, KOSPI, has already overtaken both Germany and France this year and is up 44% in 2026. Samsung and SK hynix account for nearly half the index's total weighting. The former’s share price has nearly quadrupled since the start of 2025, while SK hynix has risen roughly sixfold over the same period. These gains reflect the ongoing memory supercycle, with demand for HBM far exceeding current production capacity.

William Bratton, head of cash equity research for Asia-Pacific at BNP Paribas, told the Financial Times that, aside from ASML, European-listed equities have almost no exposure to the current AI hardware buildout. He added that South Korea could overtake the UK as well if the current rally continues.

TradingKey - The policy of Taiwan's financial regulators to relax the ceiling on fund holdings served as the catalyst for a broad rally in Taiwan stocks, and TSMC ( TSM) shares reached an all-time high as a result.

On Friday, the Taiwan Financial Supervisory Commission announced plans to increase the investment limit for local equity funds and actively managed ETFs in a single stock from the original 10% to 25%.
The primary beneficiary of this regulatory shift is undoubtedly TSMC.

TSMC's intraday share price touched a high of NT$2,190 before closing at NT$2,185, a single-day gain of 5.05%; the TAIEX simultaneously closed up 3.23% at 38,932.40 points, making the Taiwan stock market the strongest performing major index in Asia that day.

Driven by the ongoing boom in the AI industry, TSMC's share price has continued to climb, now accounting for over 44% of the TAIEX and 13% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index. The previous 10% single-stock holding limit prevented many local funds from fully positioning themselves in TSMC's rally, resulting in significant missed gains.

Vey-Sern Ling, Managing Director at Union Bancaire Privée, noted that after the holding limit is raised to 25%, local funds will have more capital to buy TSMC, which will also help narrow the discount between TSMC's Taipei-listed shares and its American Depositary Receipts (ADRs). Currently, a discount exists partly because converting Taiwan stocks into ADRs requires specific regulatory approval, whereas the U.S. market has no such restriction.

Among major markets, Canada is at new all-time highs. European indices are trading near peak levels. Across Asia, India’s Nifty 50 and Sensex are trading near records. Japan’s Nikkei 225, Taiwan’s TAIEX, Korea’s KOSPI, Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite and Singapore’s Straits Times Index are all within striking distance of their recent highs. Meanwhile China’s Shanghai Composite and the Hang Seng Index are up by 19 percent and by 29 percent year-to-date.

This broadening of leadership suggests that the global bull market is no longer driven by a handful of US AI and tech giants alone. The question now is whether the long-overlooked Philippines finally joins this global upswing.

Despite a string of negative headlines, the market has held up remarkably well. The Iglesia ni Cristo’s massive rally, calls for a withdrawal of support from the military, the resignations of the Executive Secretary and the Budget Secretary all added to the political noise.

items.t: World stocks track Wall Street's drop, erasing previous day's gains
sum: MANILA, Philippines (AP) — World stocks on Friday tracked Wall Street's sharp drop in skittish trading, with major benchmarks erasing the previous day's gains.

Worries persist about a bubble in artificial intelligence -related shares. Better than expected U.S. jobs data also have raised the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hold off on an interest rate cut in December, disappointing investors who have been counting on rate cuts to fuel more gains.
The future for the S&P 500 was up 0.2% while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged 0.3% higher.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX declined 0.9% to 23,063.05, while Britain's FTSE 100 dropped 0.5% to 9,484.29. In Paris, the CAC 40 shed 0.6% to 7,935.43.
Other big recent winners also lost ground. Bitcoin dropped 4.5% to $82,500, down from nearly $125,000 last month.

In Asian trading, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% to 48,625.88 as the government approved a 21.3 trillion yen ($135 billion) stimulus package that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi promised as part of efforts to revive the sluggish economy. However, the plans for higher government spending that would delay progress toward trimming down the national debt have put the yen and Japanese government bonds under pressure.
The yield on the 30-year government bond has been touching record levels on heavy selling, hitting 3.37% on Friday.

sum: The Hong Kong-listed shares of China's CATL, the world's largest battery maker, fell as much as 8.75% Thursday as investors sought to lock in profits, following the expiry of a six-month sales restriction on about 77.5 million shares held by early stakeholders.
The 23 cornerstone investors include Sinopec HK, Kuwait Investment Authority and UBS Asset Management, according to the company's prospectus.

CATL's IPO in May raised HK$35.7 billion ($4.6 billion) according to a company filing, reportedly making it the largest offering this year globally, as investors bet on the company's ability to ride the boom in electric vehicles. CATL shares on the Shenzhen stock exchange were also down 2.59%.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index reversed course to fall 0.47%, while the mainland CSI 300 was down 0.32%.

Other markets across the region also rose, boosted by a rally in chip shares after Nvidia's stronger-than-expected earnings and bullish forecast appeared to reinforce confidence in the global AI trade.

Shares of the chip giant jumped more than 4% in extended trading after its fiscal third-quarter earnings beat earnings and revenue expectations. The AI chip darling also gave a stronger-than-expected fourth-quarter sales forecast, with CEO Jensen Huang saying demand for its current-generation Blackwell chips is "off the charts."
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 index pared earlier gains to close 2.65% higher at 49,823.94, while the Topix index added 1.66% to 3,299.57.

Asian shares fall, tracking Wall Street’s tumble on worries about AI stocks and interest rates
sum: MANILA--Asian shares retreated on Friday, tracking Wall Street’s tumble to one of its worst days since April as Nvidia and other AI superstar stocks kept dropping on worries their prices have shot too high.
South Korea’s Kospi led the regional decline, falling 3.2% to 4,038.61 amid the global tech sell-off. Samsung Electronics shed 4.1% and SK Hynix was down 6.4%. LG Energy Solutions gave up 3.7%.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell nearly 1.7% to 50,438.99, reversing the previous day’s gains. SoftBank Group led the slide, plunging 5.7% amid losses in its technology and AI related investments.
In Chinese markets, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 1.3% to 26,732.99, while the Shanghai Composite index slipped nearly 0.2% to 4,022.89.

Data on Friday showed China’s factory output grew at a 14-month low of 4.9% year-on-year in October, down from 6.5% in September and below expectations of 5.5%. Investment in fixed asset such as factory equipment also fell 1.7% year-on-year in the January to October period.
Persisting weakness in property investments were a key factor dragging on business investment.
In Australia, the S&P /ASX 200 dropped 1.4% to 8,628.30 as hopes the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut rates faded after a strong jobs report.

IDX Closes Up 57 Points to 8,394, Hitting All-Time High on Friday
sum: Jakarta. Indonesia’s benchmark stock index climbed to a new all-time high on Friday, lifted by strong domestic sentiment despite declines across major Asian bourses.
Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) rose 57 points, or 0.69 percent, to close at 8,394, marking a new record high. The index moved in the green throughout the session within a range of 8,332–8,398.

Market data showed a trading volume of 26.1 billion shares, with a turnover of Rp 15.66 trillion ($938.18 million) and more than 2 million transactions. There were 288 gainers, 319 losers, and 202 unchanged stocks.

Across the region, shares retreated after Wall Street ended lower overnight, weighed down by losses in major technology names. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 1.1 percent to 50,276.37, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 1 percent to 26,209.16. The Shanghai Composite dropped 0.3 percent to 3,997.56, South Korea’s Kospi lost 1.8 percent to 3,953.76, and Taiwan’s Taiex declined 0.9 percent.

China reported that its exports contracted 1.1 percent in October, with shipments to the United States plunging 25 percent from a year earlier. Economists, however, expect a rebound following last week’s agreement between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to ease trade tensions.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 dropped 1.1 percent to 6,720.32, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.8 percent to 46,912.30, and the Nasdaq tumbled 1.9 percent to 23,053.99. Heavyweights like Nvidia (-3.7 percent), Microsoft (-2 percent), and Amazon (-2.9 percent) dragged the indices lower.

Meanwhile, Tesla shares fluctuated after CEO Elon Musk won a shareholder vote granting him a potential $1 trillion stock award if performance targets are met over the next decade. The stock, already up 80 percent in the past year, closed at $445.91 after rebounding in after-hours trading.

items.t: AMD outlook underwhelms investors following AI-fueled rally
sum: Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD), the main contender to Nvidia Corp in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market, failed to impress investors with its revenue forecast after an eye-popping rally sent expectations soaring.

Fourth-quarter revenue will be roughly US$9.6 billion, the company said in a statement yesterday. Though analysts had estimated US$9.2 billion on average, some projections ranged as high as US$9.9 billion.

Investors have bet heavily on AMD following blockbuster agreements with OpenAI and Oracle Corp, which plan to use the company’s chips in their build-out of AI computing. The hope is that AMD can finally crack Nvidia’s dominance in the AI processor market.
But Tuesday’s outlook signals that AMD’s payoff may come slower than some had anticipated.
The shares fell as much as 4.2 percent in premarket trading today, coinciding with a broader chip selloff driven by investors fretting that the AI boom won’t live up to expectations.

AMD stock had more than doubled this year heading into the earnings report, closing at US$250.05 yesterday. The company’s results followed a 4.1 percent decline in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index yesterday, the sharpest drop in more than three weeks.

Third-quarter sales rose 36 percent year-on-year to US$9.25 billion, beating a US$8.7 billion average estimate. Profit was US$1.20 a share, minus certain items. Analysts projected US$1.17 on average, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
